Hongtu Hu1,2,3, Zijing Zhu1,2,3, Lanlan Li 1,2,3, Jijia Hu1,2,3, Qian Yang1,2, Zhuan Peng1,2, Weiwei Li1,2, Xiaofei Cui1,2, Yanqin Fan1,2, Wenjie Chen1,2, Wei Liang 1,2 , Zhaowei Chen 1,2 & Guohua Ding 1,2

Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a major health issue, with podocyte injury with senescence playing a central role in glomerulosclerosis. This study investigates the link between glycolysis-derived serine metabolism and podocyte injury with senescence, focusing on the role of phosphoglycerate kinase 1 (PGK1) in the regulation of L-serine synthesis and podocyte homeostasis. Using in vivo and in vitro models, we examined the effects of angiotensin II (Ang II)-induced metabolic dysregulation on serine metabolism and its impact on podocyte function. The results demonstrate that Ang II downregulates PGK1 expression through the transcription factor FOXA1, leading to reduced L-serine biosynthesis, mitochondrial dysfunction, and increased cellular senescence in podocytes. Supplementing with L-serine or enhancing PGK1 expression in podocytes alleviated these pathological changes, restored mitochondrial function, and reduced senescence-associated phenotypes in CKD mouse models. Moreover, PGK1 was found to interact with keratin, type II cytoskeletal 1 (KRT1), stabilizing the cytoskeletal integrity of podocytes. These ﬁndings identify a novel metabolic pathway linking glycolysis, serine metabolism, and podocyte injury with senescence, suggesting that targeting the PGK1-serine axis may offer therapeutic potential for slowing podocyte senescence and CKD progression.

Podocytes are crucial components of the glomerular ﬁltration barrier, and their terminally differentiated nature makes them particularly vulnerable to injury. Podocyte injury is closely associated with the progression of chronic kidney disease (CKD), driven by various glomerular disorders, including hypertensive nephropathy (HN) and diabetic kidney disease (DKD)1,2. Podocyte injury triggers a cellular senescence program, resulting in a state of long-term non-proliferative cells, which ultimately leads to podocyte senescence3. Notably, podocyte senescence is a hallmark of glomerulosclerosis, as senescent podocytes contribute signiﬁcantly to the deterioration of the ﬁltration

barrier, leading to proteinuria4. Since podocytes can not regenerate, the accumulation of senescent podocytes accelerates kidney function decline5. Previous studies have identiﬁed the renin-angiotensin system (RAS) activation, particularly angiotensin II (Ang II), as a critical factor in glomerular disease progression6. However, the direct contribution of Ang II to podocyte injury with senescence and the underlying mechanisms remains to be elucidated. Recent study has highlighted the role of glycolytic intermediates in regulating essential cellular functions, such as nucleotide, lipid, and amino acid syntheses11. Among these, 3-phosphoglyceric acid (3-PG), an intermediate in glycolysis, serves as a precursor for L-serine synthesis. L-serine is pivotal in maintaining redox balance, supporting nucleotide synthesis, and modulating sphingolipid metabolism12. Notably, the kidneys are a primary organ for L-serine production, particularly during fasting13. However, the relationship between disturbed L-serine metabolism and podocyte injury and cellular senescence remains poorly understood. Phosphoglycerate kinase 1 (PGK1) plays a crucial role in glycolysis by catalyzing the conversion of 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (1,3-BPG) to 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PG), which serves as the immediate precursor for serine biosynthesis. This effect occurs independent of the activity of other serine biosynthetic enzymes, such as phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase (PHGDH) and phosphoserine aminotransferase 1 (PSAT1), suggesting that PGK1 plays a central role in serine metabolism14,15. Despite this, the role of PGK1 in Ang II-induced podocyte senescence and glomerulosclerosis has not been fully elucidated. On the other hand, the precise mechanism by which PGK1- induced L-serine metabolism contributes to podocyte damage remains to be elucidated. It has been hypothesized that L-serine may playa role in sphingolipid production as substrates16. Sphingolipids are the most abundant lipids other than cholesterol in the podocyte lipid composition, and altered sphingolipid metabolism in podocytes promotes glomerular disease17. Furthermore, recent studies have demonstrated that altered L-serine metabolism contributes to the generation of deoxysphingolipids by serine palmitoyl-transferase (SPT)18. In addition, deoxysphingolipids have been shown to contribute to actin cytoskeleton derangement as well as cellular senescence neuronal cell19. However, the potential of Ang II-induced L-serine metabolism in podocytes to induce podocyte damage and cellular senescence by affecting deoxysphingolipid production remains to be elucidated. In the present study, we aimed to investigate the molecular mechanisms in which PGK1-mediated serine metabolism contribute to Ang II-induced podocyte injury and cellular senescence. Additionally, we set out to determine whether L-serine supplementation or reinstatement of PGK1 expression can lessen renal injury in CKD mouse models, thereby presenting a therapeutic strategy to slow kidney senescence and curb CKD progression.

Results Ang II-induced serine deﬁciency, podocyte injury and cellular senescence Our previous studies have demonstrated that podocytes primarily rely on glycolysis for energy production, particularly in the foot process8. Activation of the RAS results in the inhibition of PKM2, a key glycolytic enzyme in podocytes, reducing glycolytic ﬂux. This metabolic disruption causes podocyte energy deﬁciencies, triggering actin cytoskeleton derangement and apoptosis. To further investigate the role of PKM2-mediated glycolysis in podocyte function, we measured the extracellular acidiﬁcation rate (ECAR) in podocytes under various interventions. Ang II stimulation signiﬁcantly decreased glycolytic ﬂux in podocytes. This effect was reversed by overexpression of PKM2 (Fig. 1A). Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) exert nephroprotective effects by inhibiting Ang II6. The results showed that ARB administration signiﬁcantly restored PKM2 expression in podocytes derived from patients with hypertensive nephropathy (HN) (Fig. 1B). However, ARBs

failed to fully restore synaptopodin (SYNPO) expression, indicating that Ang II-induced glycolytic disturbances may contribute to podocyte injury through additional pathways. Further RNA-seq analysis of HN patient kidney samples (GEO ID: GSE166239) revealed alterations in the amino acid biogenesis pathway (Fig. 1C), suggesting that disrupted amino acid metabolism plays a role in podocyte injury. Metabolomics analysis of podocytes subjected to Ang II, high glucose, or Adriamycin revealed signiﬁcant reductions in serine levels under all administration (Fig. 1D–F), highlighting serine as a key metabolite in podocyte dysfunction. We next examined the potential protective effects of serine supplementation in mitigating Ang II-induced podocyte injury. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) demonstrated that serine supplementation alleviated Ang II-induced mitochondrial damage in mouse podocytes (MPC-5) and human podocytes (HPC), reversing mitochondrial swelling and cristae breakage (Fig. 1G and Supplementary Fig. 1A). Flow cytometry showed that serine supplementation restored mitochondrial number and membrane potential in both MPC- 5 and HPC (Fig. 1H, I and Supplementary Fig. 1B, C). Additionally, serine supplementation improved mitochondrial function, as evidenced by increased oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and ATP production in both cell lines (Fig. 1J and Supplementary Fig. 1D, E). Serine also reversed actin cytoskeleton derangement and lipid accumulation, as demonstrated by phalloidin and Oil Red O (ORO) staining in MPC-5 and HPC (Fig. 1K, L and Supplementary Fig. 1F–H). These ﬁndings suggest that serine supplementation improves mitochondrial function and cellular structure, mitigating Ang II-induced podocyte senescence. Senescence-associated β-galactosidase (β-Gal) staining revealed a dose-dependent reduction in cellular senescence following serine supplementation (Fig. 1M and Supplementary Fig. 1I, J). Serine also decreased the secretion of pro-inﬂammatory cytokines associated with the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), including IL-1β and IL-6 (Fig. 1N, O and Supplementary Fig. 1K, L), and reduced the expression of the DNA damage marker 8-hydroxy-2’-deoxyguanosine (8-OHdG) and the cell cycle regulator p21 (Supplementary Fig. 1M, N). To further investigate the role of non-essential amino acids in podocyte senescence and function, given that previous metabolomics studies identiﬁed a reduction in proline among non-essential amino acids, we further measured changes in proline levels under various interventions (Fig. 1F). The results indicated that proline levels in MPC-5 cells were also decreased under various interventions (Supplementary Fig. 1O). To further compare the effects of proline and serine on podocyte senescence and function, we treated MPC-5 cells with Ang II in the presence of serine or proline. β-Gal staining results indicated that both proline and serine could alleviate Ang II-induced podocyte senescence, with serine showing a more signiﬁcant effect (Supplementary Fig. 1P). Additionally, phalloidin staining results indicated that proline treatment was ineffective in alleviating actin cytoskeleton derangement in MPC-5, whereas serine treatment was effective (Supplementary Fig. 1P). These results indicate that serine supplementation attenuates Ang II-induced mitochondria dysfunction, actin cytoskeleton derangement, lipid accumulation, and cellular senescence in podocytes.

Serine regulates the production of deoxysphingolipids in podocytes via the PI3K/AKT pathway To explore the mechanisms underlying serine’s protective effects, we cultured podocytes in a serine-deﬁcient medium and treated with Ang II. TEM, OCR, and phalloidin staining revealed that serine deﬁciency exacerbated Ang II-induced structural damage and impairing function in mitochondria as well as worsening actin cytoskeleton derangement (Fig. 2A–C and Supplementary Fig. 2A). To further investigate the metabolic effects of serine deﬁciency, we performed untargeted metabolomics analysis, revealing a marked alteration in metabolic proﬁles across the different treatment groups (Fig. 2E). Hierarchical clustering analysis (HCA) identiﬁed 736 signiﬁcantly altered metabolites, with lipids representing the majority of these changes (Supplementary Fig. 2F). KEGG analysis revealed that the sphingolipid biosynthesis pathway was particularly enriched in the serine-deﬁcient group, with signiﬁcant increases in deoxysphingolipid content, such as dihydroceramide (DeoxyDHCer) and deoxy-ceramide (DeoxyCer) and 1-deoxysphinganine (DeoxySA), with the highest levels of DeoxyDHCer and DeoxyCer. And this result was observed in both the serine-deﬁcient group and Ang II-treated podocytes (Fig. 2G–I and Supplementary Fig. 2G). Notably, deoxysphingolipids exacerbated actin cytoskeleton derangement and cellular senescence in a dosedependent manner, reversing the protective effects of serine (Fig. 2J and Supplementary Fig. 2H–K). Typically, deoxysphingolipids is synthesized by SPT20. By using myriocin21 to inhibit SPT expression, cellular senescence in HPC and MPC was signiﬁcantly alleviated, and the expression of p21 and 8-OHdG as well as SASP was reduced (Supplementary Fig. 2L–U). In addition, further RNA-seq analysis identiﬁed signiﬁcant changes in oxidative phosphorylation and the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway in response to serine deﬁciency (Fig. 2K, L). Furthermore, the correlation analysis of the untargeted metabolomics and RNA-seq demonstrated that the PI3K/AKT pathway was most signiﬁcantly altered in serine deﬁciency (Fig. 2M). It has been previously reported that certain amino acids are capable of binding to PI3K, thereby regulating PI3K phosphorylation22. It was therefore postulated that serine may regulate PI3K phosphorylation by binding to PI3K and thus regulating PI3K phosphorylation. Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) experiments conﬁrmed that serine directly binds to PI3K and regulates phosphorylation (Fig. 2N and Supplementary Fig. 3A). Molecular docking experiments conﬁrmed that serine directly binds to the Thr462 site of PI3K (Fig. 2O). The SPR results showed that the mutation of the T462 site of PI3K signiﬁcantly reduced the binding of PI3K to serine. In addition, PI3K activity measurements showed that serine stimulated PI3K activity by 1.8 times, while the mutation of the T462 site had no such effect (Supplementary Fig. 3B, C). To further investigate the relationship between the PI3K/AKT pathway and PGK1 and serine, we ﬁrst used CRISPR/Cas9 technology to knockout PGK1 in MPC-5 cells. Given the lethality of PGK1-/- cells, we generated PGK1+/-

cells to facilitate analysis (Supplementary Fig. 3D). Western blot analyses conﬁrmed the reduction of PGK1 protein levels in MPC-5 cells (Supplementary Fig. 3E). We further complemented PI3K-WT and PI3K- T462A overexpression plasmids in PGK1+/- cells and treated them with serine or PI3K inhibitor (Wortmannin)23. PIP3/PIP2 measurement results indicate that the T462 site mutation of PI3K does not increase the enzyme activity of PI3K. Cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA) and drug afﬁnity responsive target stability (DARTS) experiments further con- ﬁrm that the T462 site of PI3K is also critical for serine to enhance the stability of PI3K (Supplementary Fig. 3F–I). OCR and ATP measurements also showed that the mutation of the T462 site of PI3K reversed the upregulation of serine on mitochondrial function (Supplementary Fig. 3J, K). Additionally, the accumulation of deoxysphingolipids due to serine deﬁciency was mitigated by treatment with the PI3K agonist 740Y-P24, which alleviated actin cytoskeleton derangement and cellular senescence in podocytes (Fig. 2P, Q and Supplementary Fig. 3O–Q). These results demonstrate that serine regulates deoxysphingolipid metabolism in podocytes via the PI3K/AKT pathway.

PGK1 expression is downregulated in Ang II-induced podocyte injury Next, we conducted a more in-depth analysis of the de novo serine synthesis pathway. As previously mentioned, PGK1, PHGDH, and PSAT1

have been identiﬁed as pivotal rate-limiting enzymes (Fig. 3A). In order to ascertain the functions of these enzymes, we employed a short hairpin RNA (shRNA) approach to knockdown their expression in MPC- 5 cells. For this enzyme screen, each gene was silenced individually using shRNA (single-gene knockdown) rather than in combination. The results demonstrated that the knockdown of PGK1 or PHGDH had a signiﬁcant impact on serine production, but the knockdown of PGK1 signiﬁcantly decreased ATP production and podocyte senescence. Consequently, the subsequent investigations were concentrated on the function of PGK1 (Fig. 3B–D). Immunoﬂuorescence and Western blot analyses revealed that Ang II treatment downregulated PGK1 protein levels in both primary podocytes and cell lines (MPC-5 and HPC), which was accompanied by a reduction in PGK1 mRNA expression (Fig. 3E–G and Supplementary Fig. 4A–F). Additionally, analysis of single-cell RNA-seq data from patients with HN conﬁrmed that PGK1 expression was signiﬁcantly decreased in podocytes, correlating with age-related changes in serine metabolic pathways (Fig. 3H–M). Furthermore, the down-regulation of PGK1 expression was further conﬁrmed by immunoﬂuorescence and immunohistochemical staining of patient kidney tissue with HN (Fig. 3N and Supplementary Fig. 4G, H). Further clinical correlation analysis demonstrated that lower PGK1 expression was associated with increased proteinuria and albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR), decreased estimated glomerular ﬁltration rate (eGFR), and poorer prognosis, suggesting that PGK1 plays a nephroprotective role in patients with HN (Fig. 3O–S and Table S2).

PGK1 regulates the PI3K/AKT pathway in podocytes and is associated with deoxysphingolipid accumulation and cellular senescence Given that PGK1 is involved in both serine metabolism and the tricarboxylic acid cycle, we performed isotope labeling using Dglucose-13C6 to assess the impact of PGK1 knockdown on serine metabolism and tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle intermediates (Fig. 4A). PGK1 knockdown resulted in a signiﬁcant decrease in serine production and a reduction in pyruvate and TCA intermediates, including citrate (Fig. 4B–D). In addition, PGK1 knockdown also signiﬁcantly increased 1,3-BPG and reduced 3-PG contents (Fig. 4E, F). These data suggest that PGK1 participates in serine biosynthesis and plays a key regulatory role in the TCA cycle, enhancing mitochondrial respiration in podocytes. Further investigation revealed that PGK1 knockdown in MPC-5 cells led to mitochondrial structural damage, as observed by TEM, and functional impairment, as indicated by reduced OCR (Fig. 4G, H). Moreover, PGK1 knockdown exacerbated actin cytoskeleton derangement and podocyte senescence, as evidenced by increased β- Gal staining and upregulation of 8-OHdG and p21 expression (Fig. 4I, J and Supplementary Fig. 5A, B). These effects mirrored those observed with serine deﬁciency (Fig. 2C, D and Supplementary Fig. 2B, C). Untargeted metabolomics analysis of MPC-5 cells demonstrated signiﬁcant metabolic shifts in PGK1 knockdown cells, with 494 metabolites identiﬁed, the majority of which were lipids (Fig. 4K, L). Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA), KEGG pathway analysis and Western blot analyses revealed alterations in sphingolipid metabolism and the PI3K/ AKT pathway (Fig. 4M, N and Supplementary Fig. 5C–F). Furthermore, deoxysphingolipids were notably elevated in PGK1 knockdown cells (Fig. 4O). RNA-seq data further supported these ﬁndings, indicating signiﬁcant changes in metabolic and senescence-related pathways, particularly those involving the PI3K/AKT signaling axis (Fig. 4P–R). Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) further conﬁrmed that PGK1 knockdown impacts the PI3K/AKT pathway, which is associated with cellular senescence and p21 activation (Fig. 4S, T). These ﬁndings suggest that PGK1 regulates podocyte function through sphingolipid metabolism and the PI3K/AKT pathway.

Given the pivotal function of KRT1 in cytoskeleton maintenance and the established link between cytoskeleton and cellular senescence, we undertook a detailed investigation into the impact of KRT1 on cytoskeleton and podocyte senescence. Further ﬁndings revealed that KRT1 knockdown led to pronounced actin cytoskeleton derangement and a notable exacerbation of podocyte senescence, and this effect was not reversed by PGK1 overexpression (Fig. 5O–Q). Next, we further explored the dual enzymatic and non-enzymatic functions of PGK1. It has been reported that PGK1 exerts its enzymatic activity through the K13126 and T16827 sites, while protein-protein docking results indicate that PGK1 binds to KRT1 via the 200-360aa region. Therefore, we separately overexpressed PGK1-WT, PGK1-K131A, PGK1-T168A, and PGK1-Δ200-360 plasmids in PGK1+/- cells. Co-IP results showed that the deletion of the 200-360aa region of PGK1 signiﬁcantly reduced KRT1 expression, but mutations at the K131 and T168 sites had no obvious effect on KRT1 expression (Supplementary Fig. 6A). Serine content, OCR, and ATP measurement results indicated that serine production and mitochondrial function were signiﬁcantly inhibited after mutations at the K131 and T168 sites, but the Δ200-360 group showed almost no effect (Supplementary Fig. 6B–D). Additionally, β-Gal and phalloidin staining results (Supplementary Fig. 6E) further indicate that PGK1 catalytic activity is crucial for maintaining serine metabolism, mitochondrial function, and preventing podocyte senescence, while the PGK1-KRT1 interaction further regulates podocyte senescence by maintaining podocyte cytoskeletal integrity, representing an enzyme activity-independent mechanism.

Podocyte-speciﬁc overexpression of PGK1 attenuates podocyte injury with senescence in Ang II-induced mouse model To assess the in vivo role of PGK1, we generated a podocyte-speciﬁc PGK1 overexpression mouse model (PGK1podKI) by crossing PGK1ﬂoxed/

ﬂoxed mice with Podocin-Cre mice (Supplementary Fig. 7A, B). Western blot analyses conﬁrmed successful PGK1 overexpression in podocytes (Supplementary Fig. 7C). While PGK1podKI mice exhibited no signiﬁcant changes in basal renal function or pathology compared to controls, they showed signiﬁcant protection from Ang II-induced podocyte injury (Fig. 6A–E and Supplementary Fig. 7D). Serine supplementation attenuates Ang II-induced podocyte senescence in mouse models We further validated the protective effects of serine supplementation in vivo using an Ang II-induced mouse model (Supplementary Fig. 10A). We treated podocytes and mouse models with the same dose as in previous studies18, and serine supplementation restored intracellular L-serine levels to physiological ranges, with no detection of supraphysiological levels of serine in treated cells. Four weeks of serine supplementation signiﬁcantly improved renal function, as evidenced by reduced urinary ACR, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), and serum creatinine (Cr) levels (Fig. 9A–E). Histological analysis, including HE staining, SYNPO staining, TEM and scanning electron microscope (SEM), revealed that serine supplementation improved glomerular architecture, including mesangial matrix expansion, foot process damage, and podocyte cytoarchitectural integrity (Fig. 9A–E and Supplementary Fig. 10B). Serine supplementation also increased mitochondrial

function in the mouse model and primary podocytes, as indicated by enhanced OCR and ATP levels (Fig. 9F, G and Supplementary Fig. 10C, D). Further investigations revealed that serine supplementation reduced markers of podocyte senescence, including the expression of p21 and 8-OHdG, and attenuated the accumulation of lipid and deoxysphingolipids (Fig. 9I–L and Supplementary Fig. 10F). These results suggest that serine supplementation may be beneﬁcial in attenuating Ang II-induced podocyte injury with senescence in animal models.

Discussion This study highlights the critical role of the PGK1-mediated serinedeoxysphingolipid pathway in regulating podocyte injury with senescence, particularly in Ang II-induced mouse models. We further demonstrate that PGK1 is signiﬁcantly inhibited in both patients with HN and Ang II-induced mouse models. Moreover, the present study shows that PGK1 overexpression in podocytes mitigates the effects of Ang II on podocyte injury with senescence, whereas its knockdown exacerbates podocyte senescence and glomerular pathological injury. Further mechanistic studies reveal that PGK1 governs the de novo synthesis of serine and regulates mitochondrial respiration in podocytes. Additionally, we ﬁnd that serine supplementation signiﬁcantly alleviates podocyte senescence and glomerular pathological injury in Ang II-induced and non-Ang II-induced CKD mouse models, with evidence of modulation of the PI3K/AKT pathway, deoxysphingolipids production, and podocyte injury with senescence. Furthermore, PGK1 was shown to maintain cytoskeletal integrity by binding to and stabilizing KRT1. Finally, FOXA1 emerged as a key regulator of PGK1 expression, providing a novel transcriptional mechanism in Ang IIinduced podocyte injury with senescence. The activation of the RAS by Ang II is a well-established factor in the progression of CKD and has been shown to exacerbate podocyte and glomerular injury. Being terminally differentiated, podocytes are particularly susceptible to Ang II-induced damage30,31. Our previous studies have conﬁrmed that Ang II induces apoptosis and cellular shedding in podocytes, but the onset of podocyte senescence appears to precede other forms of damage, as a key event in glomerular injury8,32,33. The present study provides evidence that podocyte

senescence is an early and signiﬁcant contributor to glomerular injury in patients with HN and animal models. These ﬁndings emphasize the critical role of podocyte senescence in glomerular pathological injury and disease progression. Cellular senescence is typically characterized by irreversible proliferative arrest and is triggered by various stressors, including DNA damage, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inﬂammation34,35. Senescent cells exhibit altered chromatin structure, dysregulated gene expression, and the secretion of pro-inﬂammatory cytokines, collectively known as the SASP36,37. The present study conﬁrms that senescent podocytes exhibit elevated levels of DNA damage markers such as 8- OHdG, upregulation of p21, and impaired mitochondrial respiration. The SASP, including increased secretion of IL-1β and IL-6, was also observed in Ang II-treated podocytes, further contributing to renal aging and injury. These ﬁndings are consistent with the wellestablished role of senescence in tissue aging and suggest that targeting senescence could offer therapeutic beneﬁts in CKD. Serine, a non-essential amino acid, plays a pivotal role in numerous cellular processes, including energy metabolism, antioxidant defense, and protein synthesis12,38. It exists in two enantiomeric forms: L-serine, which is prevalent in most tissues, including the kidney, and D-serine, which is predominantly found in the brain16,39. The regulation of L-serine synthesis is crucial for maintaining cellular function, and disruptions in this pathway have been implicated in several metabolic disorders, including diabetic neuropathy, obesity, and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis18,40. Recent large prospective cohort studies suggest that serine enantiomers may serve as sensitive indicators of kidney injury, potentially exerting an effect independent of etiology41. In type 2 diabetes, a untargeted/targeted ¹H-NMR detection panel identiﬁed the serine/creatinine ratio as an early biomarker capable of distinguishing early DKD from uncomplicated diabetes42. Pediatric data further show that the D/L-serine ratio is positively correlated with creatinine and cystatin-C, and is unaffected by growth or glucocorticoid therapy, supporting its application across the entire lifespan. Finally, reduced plasma L-serine levels are associated with cognitive decline and reduced eGFR in hemodialysis patients, suggesting a systemic impact of renal serine depletion in age-related CKD43. Overall, these human studies position the PGK1-serine axis as a common metabolic checkpoint for podocyte injury and CKD progression and highlight the translational potential of measuring circulating serine as a non-invasive biomarker for risk stratiﬁcation and monitoring treatment response. In this study, our ﬁndings extend this knowledge by demonstrating that Ang II-induced podocyte senescence is associated with reduced L-serine levels and that serine supplementation signiﬁcantly reverses these effects. Moreover, we have demonstrated that serine regulates the PI3K/ AKT pathway, crucial for maintaining cellular homeostasis49,50. Inhibition of this pathway exacerbates deoxysphingolipids accumulation and podocyte senescence, while serine supplementation restores the PI3K/AKT signaling axis and alleviates these effects. This highlights a potential therapeutic target in the serine-PI3K/AKT-deoxy sphingolipid axis for mitigating podocyte senescence. PGK1, a key enzyme in glycolysis, plays a dual role in energy metabolism and serine biosynthesis51. Although much attention has been focused on the role of PHGDH in L-serine synthesis52, recent studies have shown that altered glycolytic ﬂux, rather than changes in PHGDH expression, is the primary cause of reduced serine production in disease states53. The present study demonstrates that PGK1 is essential for maintaining serine synthesis and mitochondrial function in podocytes. Knockdown of PGK1 leads to decreased ATP production, reduced serine synthesis, and increased accumulation of deoxysphingolipids, which exacerbates podocyte senescence and glomerular pathological injury. These ﬁndings implicate PGK1 as an important component of a coordinated regulatory network that integrates glycolysis with serine biosynthesis and cellular stress responses. Additionally, we have demonstrated that PGK1 interacts with KRT1, a key regulator of cytoskeletal integrity54. PGK1 stabilizes KRT1 protein, preventing its degradation and maintaining the structural integrity of podocytes. This interaction offers a new insight into the molecular mechanisms underlying podocyte injury and podocyte senescence. Moreover, we identiﬁed FOXA1 as a key transcription factor regulating PGK1 expression. FOXA1 is downregulated in response to Ang II stimulation, reducing PGK1 expression and exacerbating podocyte senescence. Rescue experiments indicate protective effects of FOXA1 are only partially dependent on PGK1, suggesting that additional PGK1-independent targets/pathways may be involved. Despite these promising ﬁndings, several limitations of the study warrant consideration. First, most of our experiments were conducted in animal models and in vitro, which may not fully replicate the complex pathophysiology of human kidney disease. Future studies incorporating clinical samples and larger patient cohorts will be necessary to validate the observed effects. Second, most untargeted metabolomics data are inferred annotations (MSI 2/3), and statistical associations alone cannot establish causality. Third, while serine supplementation shows potential, its long-term safety and effects on other organs remain unclear. Further clinical trials are required to assess the broader applicability of serine-based therapies for podocyte senescence and other kidney diseases, including DKD and hereditary nephropathies. In conclusion, our ﬁndings underscore the importance of the PGK1- regulated serine-deoxysphingolipid pathway in Ang II-induced podocyte injury and cellular senescence. PGK1-derived serine metabolism is key to maintaining podocyte function and glomerular homeostasis. These results provide a compelling scientiﬁc foundation for developing serine supplementation or PGK1 activation as a potential therapeutic strategy for CKD. Future studies focused on the regulatory mechanisms of PGK1 and its interaction with FOXA1 may offer new avenues for the treatment of podocyte senescence and kidney disease.

Methods Collection of human kidney biopsy specimens and clinical indicators Control kidney samples were obtained from non-diseased areas adjacent to cancerous tissue, whereas hypertensive nephropathy (HN) kidney samples were collected from patients with pathological changes consistent with HN, as conﬁrmed by renal biopsy. All patients were informed of the usage of their urine and blood, and written informed consent was obtained. No sex or gender analysis was performed due to the low sample size. Detailed clinical characteristics of the patients are provided in Tables S1 and S2. The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of Renmin Hospital of Wuhan University (Approval number: WDRY2023-K040).

Mouse studies Mice were housed in a pathogen-free environment with controlled humidity (40-70%), temperature (20 °C-25 °C), and a 12-hour light/dark cycle. They had unrestricted access to food and water. After the treatment period, all mice were humanely euthanized via intraperitoneal injection of sodium pentobarbital (200 mg/kg), and kidney samples were collected for subsequent analysis. The entire experimental procedure was blinded, and the Ethical Committee approved all animal experiments for the Experimental Use of Animals at Renmin Hospital, Wuhan University (Approval number: WDRM-20250602).

Establishment and treatment of Ang II-induced mouse model and non-Ang II-induced CKD mouse models Male C57BL/6 mice (6–8 weeks old, 20–25 g) were obtained from Cyagen Biosciences Co. To induce hypertension and renal injury, mice were implanted with an osmotic micropump delivering Ang II (700 ng/ kg/min) for 28 days8. Control mice received an equal volume of saline via osmotic pumps. In the Adriamycin (ADR)-induced mouse model, Male C57BL/6 mice (6–8 weeks old, 20–25 g) were injected with ADR (20 mg/kg) intravenously in the tail55. In the DKD mouse model, 16- week-old male type 2 diabetic db/db mice and genetic control db/m mice were obtained from the Cytogenes Biosciences Co.56. After the treatment period, mice were euthanized, and kidneys were harvested for further analysis.

L-serine treatment L-serine (Bio Basic Inc, SB1479) was dissolved in sterile water and administered to mice via oral gavage at a dose of 280 mg/day. Treatment began on day 0 and continued for 28 consecutive days. The treatment regimen was chosen based on previous study57 and aimed to achieve a therapeutic dose that would provide measurable effects on podocyte function and mitochondrial health.

Generation and treatment of PGK1podKI and PGK1podKO mice Podocyte-speciﬁc overexpression of PGK1 (PGK1podKI) was achieved by crossing PGK1ﬂoxed/ﬂoxed mice (C57BL/6; Cyagen Biosciences, China) with Podocin-Cre mice (C57BL/6; Cyagen Biosciences, China). For podocyte-speciﬁc PGK1 knockout (PGK1podKO), PGK1ﬂoxed/ﬂoxed mice were crossed with Cre-expressing mice (C57BL/6). Pure ﬂoxed mice from the same litter without Cre expression served as controls (PGK1ctrl). Male PGK1podKI and PGK1podKO mice (6–8 weeks old, 20–25 g) were randomly assigned to the experimental groups.

Intrarenal adeno-associated virus (AAV) delivery To investigate the effects of FOXA1 on PGK1 regulation in vivo, FOXA1 overexpression was induced by intrarenal injection of adenoassociated virus (AAV) vectors. AAV-nphs1-FOXA1 (AAV-FOXA1) and control AAV-nphs1-null (AAV-ctrl) (Hanbio Co., Ltd., China) were administered to mice via in situ renal injections at six points, four weeks before osmotic pump implantation.

Glomerular isolation Mouse glomeruli were isolated following the method described previously8. Kidneys were minced into small pieces (~1 mm3) and digested in a collagenase II, protease E, and deoxyribonuclease I solution for 30 minutes at 37 °C with gentle agitation. After digestion, the tissue was ﬁltered through 100 µm, 70 µm, and 40 µm cell sieves, and glomeruli were collected by rinsing the 40 µm sieve. Glomeruli were centrifuged at 1500 rpm for 5 minutes at 4 °C and resuspended in 5 ml of culture medium.

Podocyte culture and treatment Mouse podocytes (MPC-5) were obtained from BNCC (China) and cultured in DMEM-H medium (Hyclone, USA) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (Life-iLab, China) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin (Biosharp, China). The cells were incubated at 37 °C with 5% CO₂. A conditioned medium (serine-free ECM) was purchased from ScienCell. Conditioned immortalized human podocytes (HPC) were provided by Professor Moin A. Saleem (Southmead Hospital, Bristol, UK). Primary human podocytes were isolated as described in previous protocols8. HPC and primary human podocytes were cultured at 33 °C in RPMI 1640 (HyClone, USA) medium supplemented with 10% heatinactivated fetal bovine serum (Gibco, USA), 100 U/mL penicillinstreptomycin (Invitrogen, USA), and 1× insulin-transferrin-selenium (ITS; Invitrogen, USA). For differentiation, cells were incubated in an ITS-free medium at 37 °C for 10-14 days before treatment. Podocytes were treated with Ang II (Sigma, USA) at 10-6M for 24 hours. Cycloheximide (CHX; TargetMol, China) was used at 20 µM for 12 hours, and MG132 (TargetMol, China) at 10 µM for 8 hours. L-serine (Sigma, USA) was administered at 600 µM for 48 hours. Deoxysphingolipids (Sigma, USA) were used at 5 µM for 24 hours, and 740Y-P (TargetMol, China) at 20 µM for 24 hours.

Construction of the PGK1+/- cell line Cyagen Biosciences Co., Ltd. (China) generated the PGK1+/- cell line using CRISPR/Cas9 technology. This process included designing and synthesizing sgRNA targeting PGK1, transfecting cells, monoclonal screening, and veriﬁcation through sequencing.

Metabolic cage analysis Metabolic phenotyping was performed using the PhenoMaster system (TSE Systems) for indirect calorimetry analysis in mice. Each mouse was housed individually during the experiment. After a 2–3 days acclimatization period, key metabolic parameters such as food intake, water intake, oxygen consumption (VO2), carbon dioxide production (VCO2), respiratory exchange ratio (RER), and total activity were continuously monitored over a minimum of one week, with measurements recorded hourly.

Renal function parameter measurement Before euthanasia, blood samples were collected via orbital sinus puncture and analyzed using an automated biochemical analyzer (Beckman, USA) to measure serum creatinine (Cr) and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) levels. Mice were individually housed in metabolic cages for 24 hours to collect urine samples. Urine was centrifuged at 1000 rpm for 10 minutes at 4 °C, and the supernatant was used for subsequent analyses. The urinary albumin concentration was determined using an ELISA kit (Abcam, USA). The urinary albumin-tocreatinine ratio (ACR) was calculated by dividing the urinary albumin concentration by the serum creatinine concentration.

IL-1β and IL-6 content measurement Levels of IL-1β and IL-6 were measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits in isolated mouse glomeruli, patient serum, and treated podocyte cultures.

Cell transfection Short hairpin RNAs (shRNA) targeting PGK1, KRT1, and FOXA1 (sh- PGK1, sh-KRT1, sh-FOXA1) and a full-length PGK1 expression plasmid (OE-PGK1) were used to transfect MPC-5 cells with HiPerFect Transfection Reagent (Qiagen, Germany) and X-tremeGENE HP DNA Transfection Reagent (Roche, Switzerland). For the enzyme-screen experiment, shRNAs targeting PGK1, PHGDH, and PSAT1 were used individually (two non-overlapping shRNA sequences per gene). Knockdown efﬁciency was veriﬁed by RT-PCR and Western blot. The same transfection method was used for HPC cells. Adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors carrying the PGK1 gene (AAV-PGK1) or a control vector (AAV-ctrl) were transfected into MPC-5 cells (Hanbio Co. Ltd., China). Experiments were conducted 24 hours after transfection.

Histological and immunohistochemical (IHC) analyses Kidney tissues from both mice and patients were ﬁxed, dehydrated, and embedded in parafﬁn. Sections were dewaxed, rehydrated, and subjected to antigen retrieval. For histological analysis, hematoxylin and eosin (HE) staining was performed to evaluate renal tissue pathology. Glomerular mesangial matrix expansion was quantiﬁed by measuring the area in 30 randomly selected, non-overlapping ﬁelds per group (ﬁve ﬁelds per section). For IHC, sections were incubated with 5% bovine serum albumin (BSA) for 1 hour at room temperature, followed by incubation with primary antibodies against 8-OHdG, PGK1, and FOXA1 (all from Genetex, USA) at 4 °C overnight. Immunoreactivity was detected using HRP-coupled secondary antibodies, with diaminobenzidine as a substrate. Images were captured using an Olympus upright microscope.

Immunoﬂuorescence assay Kidney sections and podocyte membrane samples were subjected to the same preparation as for IHC. After ﬁxing the podocyte membranes with 5% BSA, sections were incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies (FOXA1, 8-OHdG, PGK1, p21, GLB1, Synaptopodin, WT1, KRT1) from Abcam (USA) and Bosterbio (China). Secondary antibodies conjugated to HRP were applied for 1 hour at room temperature, followed by nuclear staining with DAPI. Images were captured using a confocal microscope (Olympus, Japan). Average ﬂuorescence intensity was quantiﬁed in 15 randomly selected, non-overlapping ﬁelds per group (ﬁve ﬁelds per section).

ATP measurement According to the manufacturer’s instructions, ATP levels in podocytes were measured using an ATP assay kit (Beyotime, China). Absorbance was measured using a microplate reader (Bio-Rad, USA).

Oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and extra cellular acidiﬁcation rate (ECAR) assay Mitochondrial OCR and ECAR was measured using the Mitochondrial Stress Test Kit (Agilent, USA) and Glycolytic Stress Test Kit (Agilent, USA) with the Seahorse XFe96 analyzer (Seahorse Bioscience, USA), following standard procedures8.

D-glucose-13C6 stable isotope tracer analysis MPC-5 cells were cultured in a glucose-free DMEM medium supplemented with D-glucose-13C6 (4500 mg/L) for 48 hours. After treatment, cells were washed with pre-cooled 0.9% NaCl solution, extracted using methanol at -80 °C, and stored overnight. After vacuum drying, samples were stored at -80 °C for LC-MS analysis. Isotopic tracer analysis was performed using the Lipid ALL method, and 13C metabolites were identiﬁed via high-resolution LC-MS. The relative abundance of metabolites was calculated by normalizing the LC-MS peak intensities. The 13C isotope distribution for each metabolite was determined based on the peak intensities of 13C isotopes.

Serine content measurement Serine levels were quantiﬁed using an ELISA kit (Bosk-Bio). Cells were lysed with RIPA buffer and incubated with HRP-labeled detection antibody in a 96-well plate pre-coated with serine antibody at 37 °C for 1 hour. In vitro PI3K lipid kinase assay Recombinant human PI3Kα (p110α/p85α) protein was obtained from abcam. Lipid vesicles containing 5 mol% PIP₂, 40% phosphatidylcholine, 30% phosphatidylethanolamine, and 25% phosphatidylserine were prepared by freeze–thaw and extrusion (100 nm polycarbonate ﬁlter). Enzymatic reactions (50 µL) were assembled in kinase buffer (25 mM HEPES pH 7.4, 5 mM MgCl₂, 1 mM ATP, 0.1% CHAPS) containing 20 nM PI3K, 5 µM PIP₂-liposomes, and increasing concentrations of L-serine (0–1.0 mM). After incubation at 37 °C for 10 min, reactions were stopped with 50 mM EDTA, and PIP₃ production was quantiﬁed using a PIP₃ Mass ELISA kit (Echelon Biosciences) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Each condition was performed in triplicate.

Measurement of cellular PIP₃/PIP₂ Cellular phosphoinositides were quantiﬁed by LC–MS/MS. Brieﬂy, podocytes were treated with or without L-serine. Cells were lysed in methanol:chloroform:water (2:1:0.8) to extract lipids. After phase separation, organic layers were dried under nitrogen and resuspended in methanol with 5 mM ammonium acetate. Phosphoinositides were resolved on a C18 reverse-phase column and detected using a triplequadrupole mass spectrometer in MRM mode. Internal standards (C17- PIP₃ and C17-PIP₂) were used for normalization. PIP₃/PIP₂ ratios were calculated for each sample.

Cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA) MPC-5 were lysed in non-denaturing buffer (20 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 100 mM NaCl, 0.5% NP-40, 5% glycerol, protease inhibitors). Lysates (500 µg per condition) were incubated with L-serine or vehicle for 30 min at 4 °C, aliquoted, and heated for 3 min at a temperature gradient (37–72 °C, 3 °C intervals). After cooling on ice, samples were centrifuged (20,000 × g, 20 min, 4 °C) and supernatants were analyzed by SDS-PAGE and immunoblotting using anti-PI3K antibodies.

Drug afﬁnity responsive target stability (DARTS) MPC-5 lysates were prepared as above and incubated with L-serine or vehicle for 30 min at 4 °C. Pronase (Roche) was added at 1:1000 (w/w) for 15 min at 25 °C. Digestion was terminated with SDS sample buffer. Proteins were resolved by SDS-PAGE and immunoblotted for PI3K. Protein band intensities were quantiﬁed by ImageJ, and relative resistance to proteolysis was calculated.

Quantiﬁcation of deoxysphingolipids, 1,3-BPG and 3-PG Cells or tissues were homogenized in methanol and spiked with internal standards (C17-deoxysphinganine and C17-deoxysphingosine). Lipids were extracted using a Bligh-Dyer method and dried under nitrogen. Samples were derivatized with O-phthalaldehyde (OPA) where applicable and analyzed using reversephase HPLC–MS/MS on a triple-quadrupole system equipped with an ESI source. 1-deoxysphinganine (DeoxySA), 1-deoxydihydroceramides (DeoxyDHCer), 1-deoxyceramides (DeoxyCer) 1,3-Bisphosphoglyceric acid (1,3-BPG) and 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PG) were detected by MRM. Concentrations were normalized to total protein content.

β-Gal, Oil Red O (ORO) and phalloidin staining For β-gal staining, cells or kidney-frozen sections were incubated with β-gal stain (Beyotime, China) overnight at 37 °C. For ORO staining, ﬁxed cells or frozen kidney sections were incubated with ORO stain

(Thermo Fisher, USA) at 37 °C for 20 minutes. Fixed cells were incubated with phalloidin stain (Abcam, USA) for 60 minutes for cytoskeleton staining. Staining was quantiﬁed using ImageJ software.

Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and scanning electron microscope (SEM) Kidney cortex samples from mice and MPC-5 cells were collected and subjected to ﬁxation, dehydration, and embedding in epoxy resin. Mitochondrial morphology and podocyte ultrastructure were observed under TEM and SEM (Hitachi, Japan).

After blocking with 5% skim milk for 1 hour, membranes were incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies against PGK1, KRT1, FOXA1, p-PI3K, PI3K, p-AKT, AKT, and β-actin (Cell Signaling Technology, CST; Abcam, UK). HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies were applied for 1 hour, and the membranes were treated with ECL reagent (Abbkine, China).Protein bands werevisualized using a chemiluminescence imaging system (Monad, China), and the grayscale values were quantiﬁed using ImageJ software.
